title: Great addition to a great series
text:
Kudos to Angela Marsons. It’s not every author that can keep a series fresh when it lands in the double digits. But she’s done exactly that, as we reach book 14 in the Kim Stone series. Kim is no one’s idea of a shrinking violet and she has definite likes and dislikes. And one of her biggest dislikes is Tracy Frost, a reporter. So, the day doesn’t start well when she learns Tracy has been scheduled for a ride along with Kim and Bryant. But it doesn’t last long when they get a call about a horrific murder, basically a man roasted alive. And what’s weirder is that within 12 hours, his family has done a bunk.
The number of victims starts adding up and yes, I might have been one step ahead of Kim in figuring out the commonality. But it’s how Marsons spins the story that works so well. She takes you in a wild ride with twists I never saw coming. She’s done her research and she really had me thinking about all the implications. The ending has a perfect symmetry to it. And I loved seeing how Stone and Frost came together.
I highly recommend this series for those that love well done police procedural with great characters.
My thanks to NetGalley and Bookouture for an advance copy of this book.

title: There are snowflakes in Bella and Mia’s holiday kitchen! A sweet treat for the holiday season.
text:
Just in time for the holidays, Bella and Mia, have returned to their kitchen once more to share a special Italian treat with us-pizzelles.

Similar to the other books in the series, Griggs and Mulyasari have created another sugary sweet rhyming story for their readers complete with adorable illustrations.

In true form, Bella, continues to encapsulate the enthusiasm children possess when given the opportunity to help with an adult task. Her mother, Mia also perpetuates that love and attention from a parent are the best ingredients for a happy and well-adjusted child.

There was one addition to this story that will resonate with readers, the importance of sharing. In this installment friends and family arrive at Bella and Mia’s house for a surprise visit. The impromptu visit prompts the mother and daughter duo to happily share their sugary waffle cookies. Thank goodness they made so many.
Griggs carefully incorporated health and safety messages both in the story and the recipe. As with Silly Willy Apple Cake and Squishy Wishy Meatballs, she also included another of her family’s favorite recipes. This one is for Pizzelles.

Classroom Connection:

Snowflakes With Sugar would be a wonderful way to acquaint children with family holiday traditions. After a reading, children could be encouraged to share how their families prepare and celebrate the various holidays.
I could easily see this book displayed in various Pre-Kindergraten/Kindergarten classroom centers: Dramatic Play, Library, Art; and as a segue for introducing students to a tasty snack.

It would make a great addition to any Dramatic Play book bin or as the focus for a Bakery. Along with the book, spoons, bowls, aprons, empty vanilla extract bottles, etc., clipboards, pencils and paper could be added to supplement the learning fun.

In the Art Center, children could use dough, glitter and snowflake cookie cutters to create their own snowflakes with sugar. To enhance the fun and learning, youngsters could also paint a fancy snowflake and sprinkle on glitter (sugar).

title: Huge Door-Stop of a History of one of Istanbul's Most Celebrated Schools
text:
This is a large door-stop of a book, drawing on exhaustively archived materials on the history of the famous Istanbul school. Founded in the late nineteenth century by American missionaries, it gradually grew into a cosmopolitan community attracting learners from a variety of social, cultural, and ethnic backgrounds. Often causing controversy, especially during the last days of the Ottoman Empire on account of its pro-western orientation, the school nonetheless survived by offering a diet of languages, an humanities education, and a pluralistic outlook on life that often contradicted the prevailing ideology on monotheism and unity of nationality.

In the Kemalist era the school's policies changed. There was a palpable shift away from multiculturalism into a more pronounced emphasis on nationalism and unity of nation. This was only to be expected in an emergent Republic where governments were concerned to encourage support for the fledgling regime. Sometimes this led to controversy between the ruling school oligarchy and the government forces trying to regulate them, but in the end Robert College managed to survive through a combination of educational cunning and sheer bloody-mindedness.

SPIRITUS ROBERTI tells a fascinating tale of how Turkish cultures evolved at the end of the Ottoman Empire and at the beginning of the Republic. It talks of the often problematic relationship between western and eastern interests, and how the presence of the foreigner within late Ottoman society often causes suspicions, especially among the more traditional noble people. Nonetheless the presence of some often clever administrators within the school ensured its continued existence.

Although exhaustively researched, Orlin Sabev's work lacks clarity of argument. Sometimes it seems that he is so concerned to pack as much research material into his narrative that his storyline often become occluded by fact. Readers are left to pick there way through a mass of verbiage in order to identify the main thematic strands of the book. For a better history, readers should be better advised to read George Washburn's account of the origins of the college, published early in the previous century but reissued by Bosphorus University Press in 2009. SPIRITUS ROBERTI also contains irritating proof-reading errors that could have required greater attention .

title: Decently written  and occasionally effective, but rather boring, pointless, and absurd
text:
I picked this up because several people have recently told me that it's their favorite book...and after reading it, I frankly can't imagine why. Very little actually happens for the first three-quarters of the novel...it's all mood, which the events of the story simply don't justify. It's all in the narrator's head, just her own endless, causelessly fearful flights of fancy, which makes her very difficult to like, or even sympathize with. When the plot does pick up in the last quarter of the novel, it becomes absurd.

*SPOILER ALERT*

"Oh, by the way, dear, I actually murdered my first wife." "Oh, well that's a relief!" "The shameless hussy told me she got herself knocked up by another man, so I shot her." "Oh, I don't mind your reasons, I'm just glad you hated her!" "Unfortunately, it looks like my crime may be exposed after all." "Let me help you cover it up, darling!" Suddenly, she is no longer her old useless self...and the ostensible reasons for this don't make any sense, even on the novel's own terms. Oh, and Mrs. Danvers has got to be one of the lamest beloved villains in all of literature...why the hell didn't they just give her the sack several times over?

The whole thing was rather boring, absurd, and pointless. Apart from the plot and character inconsistencies, it is decently written, and it is quite effective in places---but it isn't remotely in the same league as gothic novels like Jayne Eyre or the sensation novels of Wilkie Collins in whose tradition it is often placed.

Two and a half stars.

title: Awesomely Dark and Rich Novella
text:
"The God Engines" is dark, heavy, and richly textured beneath a gauze of foreboding. John Scalzi's novella is a severe departure from the tone and wit of his popular "Old Man's War" series. But it's equally as awesome.

The title is quite literal. Superhuman god-like beings are the engines that drive human interstellar travel. While they have the power to move humans and ships across enormous amounts of space, their powers are much more vast. The story moves at a rapid pace, and the characters are well drawn despite the books' length. The universe of "The God Engines" is creatively conceived.

Scalzi's story, which sits somewhere between scifi and fantasy, takes an compelling look at religion, faith and what they can really mean to individuals and societies. The foundation of characters are military, like much of Scalzi's "Old Man's War", but this military and this universe is much more frightening.

Everything is drawn with muted colors. Scalzi's writing is very clear, and always crisp, but one can't help but feel a little suffocated in reading this story. Scalzi is also a master at forwarding a plot through well-worded and well-timed dialogue.

This is not your father's John Scalzi. And this is very good.

title: heartfelt memoir but felt rushed
text:
I listened to this audio (4.5 hours) twice, alone and then on a road trip with the hub. We both enjoyed it as we are long time Jeopardy fans who were saddened to learn in March of 2019 that Alex Trebek had been diagnosed with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer.

The memoir is read mostly by Ken Jennings, an all-time champ (winning 2 million plus) from the show. He is now close friend of Trebek. Alex does read the intro and wrap up as well as a few smaller parts in between. All of the chapters about his life start out in the form of a question, much like the game show.

Trebek was raised along with his younger sister in a working class Canadian household. He's a Mr. Fix-it type who always liked to putter around the house and admits that he has a 3-car garage full of tools and gadgets, some he was never quite sure how to use. He's also a charitable man, a real humanitarian who believes deeply in helping the less fortunate, humans and animals alike. He doesn't feel that wealthy people, including himself, need a tax break and that they should pay their fair share so that more of less fortunate can be helped. Married to his second wife, Jeanie, for 30 years, (she is 24 years younger) the couple has 2 adult children together. Although they've traveled quite a bit, Alex also admits to enjoying a simple life: home, family and relaxing outdoors.

Trebek admits that he never wanted to write a memoir and had been approached many times earlier. However, after his cancer diagnosis, he agreed as he didn't want an unauthorized bio written after he passes away. 100% of the proceeds of this book will be donated to a variety of organizations important to Trebek.

Although we enjoyed listening to this memoir, at times it didn't feel like a lot of thought was put into it. Perhaps the book was a bit rushed because of the seriousness of his illness.

title: Excellent, unique bible
text:
The New Illustrated Bible of Jerusalem is published by Sacralion Publishing House. The Lockman Foundation, who publishes the New American Standard Bible was very kind to provide me with a review copy of this bible. It contains the NASB Update text, which happens to be one of my favorites.

This particular bible is unique in that it contains 436 old photographs of Jerusalem and other bible-related places. These pictures are very interesting and are placed near pertinent verses in the bible. They are all black and white, but the pictures are very crisp and clear.

As mentioned earlier, this bible contains the updated NASB text. I was very pleased to see that they chose the exact same text layout as the Lockman NASB Large Print Ultrathin Bible with happens to be one of my favorites. The text is about 10 point font and is very clear and legible. This layout also has 95,000 cross-references which are very helpful. The page numbers are different due to the added pictures. The paper in this bible is excellent. There is very little ghosting (text showing through the pages) due to the weight of the paper.

This is a big bible. It has a similar footprint (6.75"x 9.75") to the ESV Study Bible, but it is actually thicker (2.75"). It is a hardback covered with imitation leather. The decorative images stamped into it give it the look of the old family bibles from the late 1800's.

This bible has a concordance as well as old testament genealogical tables in the back which should prove to be useful.

Overall, I am very happy with this bible. It has a solid sewn binding, excellent paper, and dark clear printing. If you are looking for a unique bible or you like big bibles, you should consider this one.

Disclosure of material connection: The Lockman Foundation provided a free copy of this bible for me to review. I was not required to provide a positive review.

(Because we are both parents and early childhood and elementary educators, we may be more attuned to and concerned about role models in books, which may not be as big of an issue or concern to others so this book may be fine depending on one's particular sensitivies and orientation.) Not every child is a childhood prodigy like Farkle McBride and particularly with certain issues that surround children in today's American culture and media, I am concerned about a child being exposed to a character who can master something without trying that hard or practicing or sticking to it and who easily gives up what they're doing because they get bored. Though not automatically negative, there's a bit of concern that a message is being sent suggesting that the one who is in charge (e.g. the conductor) has a better job than the others. Though amusing from an adult point of view, the book has images of instruments being broken in pieces or thrown away because the child is bored of them - not a good model for caring for personal property and respecting the investment (monetary and time) made by his parents to support his interests. We love Lithgow's other children's CDs and some of his other works but considering the selection of books out there, I think one can easily make a better choice for stories about children and music (e.g. for whole orchestra books try "Zin, Zin, Zin, A Vioin", the Gustav Mole books, "The Hippo Hop", "The Story of the Incredible Orchestra", and for less than full orchestra books, "Mole Music", "Song and Dance Man").

title: An okay novel but the plot is not cooked well
text:
This book is my first encounter with a novel Harry Hunsicker. The protagonist Jonatahn Cantrell working as a problem-solver for a law firm is asked to find a missing African American boy and then a trouble starts falling on him. The deputy chief of Dallas Police, who secretly confided in him to conduct the search, appears to be hiding some important information from him, and his confrontation with him, who happens to be dating a former lover and job partner Piper, results in altercation. In the meantime there is a serial killer eliminating high-level Dallas criminals. The story unfolds with three major questions in play, "Where is the boy?", "What is the deputy chief hiding from Jonathan?", and "Who is the killer?", and is told from four angles: from Jon's perspective (first person), snapshots of key events in the deputy's life (third person), killer's attacks from victim's view points, and an aggressive SWAT officer who may have some grudge against the deputy. The three questions are answered, but some other peripheral riddles. such as why the deputy chose to perform covert operation and why he picked him for the operation, are left answered. The reader of course can make pretty good guesses about them (except one, which is why the serial killer chose to kill those people), but it would have been more helpful and convincing had the answers been given explicitly.

The major weakness of this work is that there are too many view points are used with none being fully exploited. There are also references to the past incidents between Jonathan and Piper, which may appear in the first book of the series, but the lack of details of those incidents, in combination with the non-extensive exploration of the view points, result in some frustration on the reader.

This is a fun and informative book for kids concerning the Bible published by Harvest House Publishers. I went through this book together with my kids at night and they enjoyed the pictures, graph and facts. The subtitle of the book reveals some of the contents covered in this book: Light and Dark, Heroes and Villains, and Mind-Blowing Bible Facts. In addition there’s also “Wonders of the Biblical world,” “Epic Battles of the Bible” and “Biblical Landmarks.” My favorite sections of the book was the discussion and infographics on the Trinity and Jesus’ incarnation. It was very biblical and also covered common pitfalls of analogies people try to use to describe the Trinity. Yet it did it in a manner that was easy (as much as possible) for kids to understand while being biblically solid. The proof of the humanity and divinity of Christ was also well laid out. I must also give props to the writers for covering also the topic of heaven and hell. Sometimes it seems kids book can be quite shallow in terms of being faithful to the Word of God so for a kids book to actually handle the topic of hell faithfully while also being conscious that kids are reading this book that is no small feat to pull off. Kudos to the publishers, writers and illustrator! Also I am glad that the book does share the Gospel as well.
Kids will enjoy the pictures and graphics. As a pastor I approve of the biblical content in being faithful to Scripture, historically accurate and accessible for any parents as a general reading audience to read and explain to their kids. Well done, and I hope there’s a future third volume in this series.

title: An Entertaining Installment In The Perry Mason Series
text:
Erle Stanley Gardner (1889-1970) wrote more than one hundred novels over the course of his long career. A trial lawyer himself, Gardner's best known creation was Perry Mason, a flamboyant criminal defense attorney who earns his large fees by virtue of a remarkable talent for using the law to uncover the truth on the witness stand.

In this particular instance Mason is retained by a woman who asks him to cross-examine her husband about a peculiar story he has told--a story involving an attractive and sadly stranded motorist that he rescued the night before. What interests Mason is the fact that Mrs. Kirby isn't the jealous type; she's only concerned that her husband may have fabricated the story in order to get himself out of a possibly dangerous scrape. And unfolding events show that she's right on target. It isn't long before a body surfaces and Mr. Kirby is in the hands of DA Hamilton Burger.

The Perry Mason novels are pure genre, but they are genre fiction at its best, and while the laws (and certainly forensic science) has changed over the years they are still fun to read. Erle Stanley Gardner was at the peak of his powers in the 1950s, and while this 1957 novel is a shade too preachy for its own good it remains a lot of fun. Recommended.

title: In other words, we're doomed.
text:
The authors of this book are both professors in Christian stuff and both have many years of pastoral ministry experience. In this book, they’ve convinced me that churches are basically doomed.

The first 130 of 248 pages introduced the concept of “identity” and put me through a crash-course in social psychobabble. I found a few interesting thoughts here, but I felt like I had to plow through way too many words to get them. The bottom line is that Christians are supposed to be different, and the church is supposed to be full of Christians, but the Christians in the church are different too.

(According to the authors I have multiple identities, and I suppose that is true in the eyes of others, but to myself I have one identity comprised of several core attributes. This one identity plays different roles, and those roles have changed in priority over time. Perhaps I’m just a simple creature.)

Over half-way through the book we get specific treatment of the things that actually divide people.

Chapter 6 on Race, Ethnicity, and Identity takes us through a predictable discussion of certain passages in Paul’s letters where significant differences in ethnicity were dealt with by creating a super-ordinate identity in Christ that supersedes (my word) those identities while leaving those ethnic identities intact. Fine, but I already knew that. (I did appreciate the observation that the problem with the Lord’s Supper in 1 Corinthians was that many in this church had not completely transitioned from their pagan identity to their Christian identity. I’d never heard or read it put so simply before.)

Chapter 7 on Neither Male nor Female went to great lengths to describe the current state of our culture, which anyone who hasn’t been asleep for twenty years should already know, but provides no solutions other than a sexually/biblically correct Christian might invest a huge amount of time over years in a non-biblical person, and they might come to saving faith and to the biblically correct church.

Chapter 8 on Generational Differences, after stereotyping boomers and every generation since (with some accuracy I’ll grant), offers its primary solution as the old should get out of the way and let the younger take over, something that aging and death make inevitable anyway.

Chapter 9 just told me that Christians have lost the culture war and that we may as well get accustomed to living as outsiders in a country where we weren’t outsiders a couple generations ago. On page 177, the authors write, “The culture-war strategy also requires a level of organization and media presence that is beyond the reach of most churches.” Really? I follow YouTube channels where individuals are waging the culture war for free from their bedrooms and have over 1 million subscribers. Well, there’s one reason why the church lost the culture war.

The Final Thoughts were little more than a rehash of what I had just read. I felt like for the pages I read I got very little out of this book. Much just stated the obvious and predictable, with ten-dollar social psychology words thrown in. There were many paragraph-long anecdotal stories, but the only case studies came from 1 Corinthians, not the life experience of the authors of this book. I expected some detailed, real-life case studies of church conflict resolution, but there were none. This book was generalities for problems with vague suggestions for solutions, but nothing put into practice with genuine, documented results. It was pretty much all together different from what I expected.

title: The Little Picture
text:
Alan T. Nolan in the Introduction to "Brave Men's Tears"says, "the little pictures must be examined in order for one to construct the big picture." This book should meet his idea of the "little picture". A good detailed tactical history of one of the smaller battles. A history that is well written, easy to read presenting a vivid picture of battle. This book has all of these things but contains some real drawbacks.
It is hard to find anything positive about the Battle of the Crater. This was one of the worst episodes of the Civil War. Political considerations overruled military considerations. The questions it caused about personal feelings and possible rivalries within the Union high command are still being raised. In addition, this battled exposed very real personal problems at the division and corps level in the Army of the Potomac. The Crater resulted in five thousand causalities, two inquires, a stain on Meade's record and was a major factor in the removal of Burnside from command of the IX Corps. The hole is still visible over 140 years later and cannot fail to move any student of the war.
This book has one map of the mine to the Confederate lines, which is not a problem. The battle is at close-quarters in and around the crater and in the adjacent trenches. The author's description is enough to convey the battlefield more vividly and completely than a series of maps would. This is one of the rare battle histories where maps are not required.
Alan Axelrod indicts General Meade for sabotaging Burnside's plan. He asserts this starts in 1862, when Burnside is Meade's commanding officer at Fredericksburg. Meade's rise to command and Burnside being placed under him are used to prove his contention. The author tries to demonstrate that Meade has no respect or confidence in Burnside and undercuts him at every opportunity. This theme is the main storyline, continually popping up in an attempt to convince the reader by repetition. The author should follow the format of "Plenty of Blame to Go Around", tell the story, present the controversy, give your view and let the reader decide. No one made good decisions here. However, assuming Meade's motivation is personal pique requires more than the author offers.
My second problem is the importance attached to this battle. The author feels that victory here would have ended the war saving tens of thousands of lives. He consistently overstates the importance of the battle and the benefits that victory could have produced. In doing so, he ignores every theater but Virginia and encourages the ides that the surrender of Lee's army ended the Civil War.
One the plus side, this book contains a good discussion of Civil War combat fatigue and how it is not being addressed by the high command. The treatment of the United States Colored Troops at the Carter is factual without being judgmental. The author simply states the problems and the results they produced without moralizing or condemning either side. This approach is more powerful and drives home the problems these men faced is the strongest possible manner. The description of the battle is vivid, direct and the best part of the book. Working with an excellent understanding of the tactical details, we are walked through what has to be one of the worst battles a Union solider could have been in.

title: A History Lessons Demonstrating the Value of Integrity, Loyalty, Friendship, and Hard-work
text:
I titled this review as, "A History Lessons Demonstrating the Value of Integrity, Loyalty, Friendship, and Hard-work" which seems both lofty and a bit preachy... however, for "Becoming Teddy Roosevelt" it is a perfect fit. The story of Teddy Roosevelt's rise from being a weak sickly (but wealthy) boy from New York, to leader of the Rough Riders, to President of the United States is one of the most fascinating transformations in American history (if not THE MOST fascinating.... the others that come to mind are Alexander Hamilton, Abe Lincoln, and Harry Truman). The man who was most responsible for this transformation (outside of Roosevelt himself) was Bill Sewall.

Side Note: I am typically offered 3-4 books a day by authors for reviewing consideration. Due to time constraints, I am usually required to reject 99% of the requests. In the case of"Becoming Teddy Roosevelt" I found time to read a copy, and I am very thankful that I did.

Back tot he book.... Andrew Vietze writes from a perspective of authority. This is not a crusty historian writing about Roosevelt and Sewall's passion for the outdoors. This is a passion that Vietze shares and it allows him to capture the perspective and share their enthusiasm for the Maine wilderness. To my knowledge, no one has written a book that is so effective in demonstrating the relationship between Roosevelt and Sewall and their mutual love of the outdoors.

The story of Roosevelt and Sewall would be interesting even if Roosevelt hadn't become president. However, as Roosevelt it is clear that time, work, and experiences shared with Sewall helped to shape the policy of the 26th President. The results influenced his ability to lead the Rough Riders - to his founding of the National Parks Service which ultimately became his lasting legacy.

Final Verdict - An absolute read for any fan of Teddy Roosevelt. However, I also recommend it to all lovers of the outdoors and our National Parks. A easy recommendation - probably the best book I have read in the last 12 months.

5 Stars

title: Smaller isn't necessarily the lesser / Guts can come in any size
text:
In the past, determining a bias in the publication of folk and fairytales was a fairly straightforward business. Too many European maids of hair as fair as the silk of corn on your shelves? Bias. But now we’re in the thick of a downturn in the publication of folk and fairytales. We not only need diverse fairy and folktales but we need more fairy and folktales at all! If you can find more than twenty published in a given year, that’s considered a good year. But desperation can lead to poor choices. A librarian might clutch at straws and snap up any such story, just so long as it fulfills a need. In the case of the latest adaptation of the story of Issun Bôshi to the picture book format, however, put your mind at rest. You rarely find such a meticulous combination of stunning art and melodic text as located here. Adapted from a Japanese folktale, “Issun Bôshi” by Icinori is a stunner. Regardless of whether or not you collect fairy and folktales, you need this on your shelf. Stat.

“We’d like a little boy, any size at all. / We’d like him little, we’d like him small. / We’d love him tiniest of all.” Be careful what you wish for? Not really. When a childless peasant and his wife sing this song on their walk to and from the fields where they toil they are nothing but delighted when the wife gives birth to a kid that would give Stuart Little a run for his money. A clever fellow, Issun Bôshi (for so he is named) grows up and when the time comes he sets off to seek his fortune with just a needle and a rice bowl to his name. Along his travels he is waylaid by a fowl and tricky ogre. Issun Bôshi leaves him and continues further, but when a nobleman’s daughter is taken by that same sneaky demon, it is Issun Bôshi and his incredible size that saves the day once and for all.

Think of all the great fairytales and folktales that involve little people. You’ve your straight fairytales like Thumbelina and Tom Thumb. Your tall tales like “Hewitt Anderson’s Great Big Life” and folktales like “Pea Boy”. That’s not even mentioning all the tales of elves and dwarfs and what have you. It hardly matters what culture you’re in. Little people, ridiculously little people, are a storytelling staple. I suppose tiny people make for instantaneous identification. Haven’t we all felt insignificant in the face of our great big world at some point in our lives? Wouldn’t we love it if we could overcome our shortcomings (ha ha) and triumph in the end? One of the interesting things about Issun Bôshi is that by the end of the tale he does attain tall status but only as a last resort. When offered height earlier in the tale he shows no interest whatsoever. Sure, he’d like to prove to the nobleman’s daughter that he’s more than a living doll, but as the ending of the book notes, “People say that Issun Bôshi sometimes misses being small.” Read into it whatever you want (missing childhood, missing the simple life when you’ve become “big” in the world, etc.).

The art of the picture book translation is such that as an American who essentially speaks just one language, I am in awe. I’ve also read enough stilted, awkwardly translated books for kids to know when a book is particularly well done. All we know about the translation of “Issun Bôshi” is that the publication page says “Translation of French by Nicholas Grindell & Co. (Berlin & Ryde)”. So who knows whom the genius was who worked on this book! Whoever it was, it was someone who knew that this folktale would have to be read aloud many times, often to large groups. Heck, the very last line of the book is so beautiful and subtle that I’ve gone back to it several times. It reads, “People say that the nobleman’s daughter has taken a different view of Issun Bôshi and that their story is not yet over.” I vastly prefer that to a romantic ending or even the old standard “and they lived happily ever after.” This ending suggests that there could be more adventures to come and that their fate is not as fixed as your standard folktale would assign. Heck, we don’t even know for certain that they become romantically involved.

Text text text. What about the art? Because it seems to me that in this world you’re often only as good as the pictures that accompany your tale. The author/illustrator of this book is listed only as the mysterious one-namer “Icinori”. Naturally I had to learn more and so in the course of my research (research = looking up information about the publisher) I discovered that Icinori actually two artists. On the one hand you have Mayumi Otero, a French illustrator. On the other you have Raphaël Urwiller, a graphic designer and illustrator. No word on who precisely was responsible for the wordplay here. All we really know is that for this book the art appears to consist of beautiful prints. The Japanese artistic influence is clear, though Icinori has come up with a very distinctive look of their own overall. The primary colors in the palette consist of blue, orange, and yellow. Best of all, there’s time for two-page silent spreads of pure unadulterated beauty. For example, once Issun Bôshi has set out to see the world the story slows down enough for you to witness a gorgeous river landscape, the water and sky a pure white while all around vegetation and animals vie for your eye. I love too how Icinori isn’t afraid to shift scenes between a busy city street scene and the tri-colored drama of Issun Bôshi being dropped down an ogre’s gullet.

There is a sense of relief that one feels when a book turns out to sound as good as it looks. Covers can be misleading. A title that looks like a gem on the outside can yield particularly dull or overdone results inside. “Issun Bôshi”, I am happy to say, never disappoints. It skips, it hops, it dives, it sings. It entertains fully and leaves the reader wanting more. It does not, therefore, ever come across as anything but one of the finest folktale adaptations you’ve ever seen. High praise. Great book. Must buy.

title: Unhappy Professor Parini
text:
Mr. Steiner's review diagnoses perfectly the problem with Professor Parini's book - Professor Parini. The writer is brilliant and his book is useful, but his frequent unsupported allegations and (occasional) surprisingly shallow opinions do become tiresome. His ill-mannered behavior regarding his invitation to the White House is Look-at-Me posturing that would quite properly embarrass an adolescent. I genuinely disapprove of President Obama's policies, but if I were invited to visit him I would never presume to demand that my agenda take precedence over good manners. Finally, Mr. Steiner is bang-on about Professor Parini in this: like many college instructors and professors the author is a master of the mechanics and of sources, but in the end doesn't seem to like poetry.

Surely when Professor Parini was but Jay, a young man in the springtime of his life, he delighted in poetry. He could have made a better effort to keep something of that joy instead of surrendering to the querulousness of old age.

title: This Book Of Political Quotes Has Its Moments, But It Was Just Okay For Me As I Didn't Find It Consistently Entertaining
text:
This book is supposed to be a collection of the "funniest, dumbest, most outrageous" comments by our leaders throughout history. The Founding Fathers, Democrats and Republicans as groups get whole chapters, and a chapter is devoted to each of George W. Bush, John F. Kennedy, Sarah Palin and Jesse Ventura himself. The rest of the book is broken down by topic and mixes quotes from various leaders. A brief context is provided with the listed quotes, though there's little writing here beyond the quotes themselves (as expected). I think there's a wide variance on who will enjoy this book that may depend on different factors- like how well versed and interested one is in politics, one's sense of humor, what political party one affiliates with, whether one is a Jesse Ventura fan or not, and so on.

This is the first book I've read by Ventura. For me, I just thought it was okay. Maybe I'm humorless or not political enough for all the quotes to make sense, but at times the quotes just didn't resonate with me as being fun, dumb or outrageous. I read many out loud with family and most of the time none of us laughed or were very entertained. I guess I expected to laugh or be surprised more. I did get a kick out of some quotes, especially those pertaining to the Founding Fathers. But other quotes were by politicians I'm too unfamiliar with, while others were by Presidents and politicians of my time that I'm so familiar with I practically know the outrageous and dumb quotes by heart, such as Bill Clinton comments about Monica Lewinsky.

I'm a registered voter who switched parties mid life, and I'm not sensitive about jabs taken at either political party- so my political affiliation did not factor into my enjoyment. I just could only read the book in small doses, and it was such a mixed bag of entertaining quotes mixed with quotes that evoked no reaction from me. Maybe it's the presentation, or perhaps it's just my own cynicism or brand of humor (or lack thereof), but I just didn't find the book consistently entertaining. Or perhaps I'm all too aware of some of the biggest blunders of Presidents and candidates of my time, so the outrage factor was diminished. I also think some quotes just seemed like nitpicking a leader's obvious accidental misuse of a word and just weren't that funny.

Maybe a few examples will help readers decide if this book will be entertaining. One example is JFK said: "We must use time as a tool, not as a crutch." I honestly don't know what to make of the comment being in this book as I'm not sure how that fits into funny, dumb or outrageous- so I guess I'm dense or missing something- and I had the same reaction to many others. On the other hand, it's clearly outrageous that Joe Biden said: "You cannot go to a 7-11 or a Dunkin' Donuts unless you have a slight Indian accent...I'm not joking." And, of course, it's just a slip of the tongue but kind of funny for Al Gore, in referring to George H. W. Bush, to say a "zebra does not change its spots." And I've always gotten a kick out of Gore's statement that he "took the initiative in creating the Internet" and still do, so that's funny to me.These are just a few examples. I think some people will love this book, some will hate it and others like me will just think it's okay.

This book is quick and has a short list of recipes per chapter. It's amazingly simple and makes me think the author did not do his research appropriately. The reason for this is that Africa is not a country it's a continent and there are all sorts of recipes for all sorts of things in AFrica, it's not fair to say that this zucchini, carrot, peanut and ginger soup is made in Africa, I am sure it's only made in one region of Africa and not the entire continent the same for anything in India. I would expect the author to do more research before putting this book together and find out what region of Africa, China and India these recipes come from. It bothers me when a book is put out without the necessary research to make it authentic and I believe this is not authentic in nature as the recipes are also found in the another cook book I have in print.

title: Contrived Situation and Obvious What's Happening
text: Agatha Christie's 1952 "Miss Marple" novel (the 5th novel in that series (I don't know why Amazon says it's the 6th)), "[[ASIN:B000FC1PLG They Do It With Mirrors: A Miss Marple Mystery (Miss Marple Mysteries Book 6)]]," suffers from some serious problems.  First, the setting is so contrived that you can feel Christie trying to cram the situation into the book.  Worse, she's apparently aware of how contrived it is since she has a character come right out and complain about it.  Second, and most seriously, what's going on is so obvious that by the time the murder actually occurs, I knew what was happening (and just as importantly, what was NOT happening).  And finally, some of her characterizations are getting stale.  For instance, her American character in this book is pretty much the same shallow caricature of Americans that she included in her books from the 1920s.  The same holds for just about all the nationalities she uses.  Thirty years of such bad characterizations is just too much.  So, I'm rating the book at a Pretty Bad 2 stars out of 5.

text: This is only my second Damita Victoria book.  This book is very "cute," as the title implies.  My favorite images are the lovely little house scenes. I'm not a huge fan of the multiple catch lights (highlights) in some of the girls' eyes.  I'm also not a fan of the crosses in some of the scenes.  I know crosses are one of the stereotypical Halloween iconography, but I'd just as soon wish they weren't present.  The images are printed as single-sided pages, with reverse black sides.  Each image is unique, with no duplicates.  I think I counted a very generous five color test and swatching pages, in a couple of formats. I sort of miss the very subtle grayscale of "Adorable Cuties," but I think the vocal minority have ruined that for those that liked it in "easy" books.  A few marker users complained that it gets in their shading, when as "artists," several don't really even do much shading.  I'm not a self-styled "artist," so I appreciated the subtle help. title: An unsung superstar
text:
There's an old saying, mentioned in this book, that goes: "If you can remember the sixties, you weren't really there!" For those of us who were there and actually can remember, this book is a delightful nostalgic tour.

Dave Van Ronk was a central figure in the huge folk music craze of the early sixties. He was also an important figure in the jazz and blues scene that preceded and, in large part, begat the folk phenomenon. Although he spent a small period of time on the west coast, his primary haunt was the Greenwich Village scene in New York. This book was originally intended to be an insider's account of that scene and the folk music genre that largely originated from there.

Unfortunately, Dave died before the book was finished. His co-author, Elijah Wald, took over, collected and organized Dave's notes and interview recordings, and produced what is as much a biography of Dave Van Ronk as it is about the folk scene. In the process, we are treated to first-hand accounts of some real giants of the movement, like Pete Seeger; Bob Dylan; Tom Paxton; Joni Mitchell; Peter, Paul & Mary; Jose Feliciano, as well as legendary blues artists; Gary Davis, John Lee Hooker, Muddy Waters, Mississippi John Hurt, among many others.

Van Ronk himself was a die-hard ethnic purist who sincerely admired those he considered to be the true greats and precursors to the movement. He was not reticent in voicing his criticisms of the more trivial aspects of the folk music movement. There's more than a hint of jealousy in many of his comments about some of the artists who "made it big," e.g., the Kingston Trio, Harry Belafonte, etc. However, if the reader takes what he says with a grain of salt, there's a huge amount of fascinating information in this book about not only an amazing period in the history of American music, but a transcendent period in American culture. There are fascinating anecdotes on virtually every page.

If you're too young to remember the sixties, this book is a great introduction. If you were actually there (but, of course, can't remember), it will jar your memory and stoke your nostalgia. Highly recommended.

title: Beautiful story of a daughter searching for her mother
text:
Jenna is a 13 year old girl searching for her mother and is determined to find her. Jenna is the young daughter of two brilliant scientists, Thomas and Alice. Both parents work with elephants at a sanctuary for elephants in New Hampshire. One day something goes horribly wrong and suddenly Alice is gone. Jenna has lost her mother at the age of three and now is determined to find her mom.

Jenna finds a psychic to search for her mother, well a lapsed psychic, but a psychic, nonetheless. The psychic, Serenity, and another enlistee, a private eye named Virgil, set out with Jenna to look for Alice. Virgil worked for the local police department when ten years earlier, Jenna's mom disappeared.

Each chapter is told from the point-of-view of Alice, Jenna, Virgil and Serenity. Each chapter spools out the mystery of what has happened to Alice. The elephants and their stories also are a major part of the book.

I loved this book on so many levels because of the elephant's stories and how they came to the New Hampshire elephant sanctuary and for the stories of Serenity, Jenna, Alice and Virgil. The ending is bittersweet and I had tears in my eyes. A beautiful story that will haunt you when you the reach the conclusion.

title: Got Fear?  Get Some Nerve.
text:
Tired of being an "armchair adventurer"? Want to take more risks and experience more joy? Want to face your fears? "All you need is 'some nerve'," says this author, Patty Chang Anker, to start your journey towards a more expansive life. The number one antidote to fear is experience says this book. The author, an almost-40 former publicist-turned-yoga-instructor and mother, decides to try experiences she has been avoiding to dissolve her fears.

Written in a lively and droll style, this book details the new experiences she tries, the lessons she takes, the books she reads for some expert coaching on overcoming specific fears. "I am going to start saying yes to things that scare me," she tells herself.

Activities she starts saying yes to include diving lessons, riding a bike, public speaking, surfing in the winter on Lake Michigan, and self-defense classes among others. She also helps others overcome their fears. She references Benjamin and Rosamund Zander's book THE ART OF POSSIBILITY in which Zander has his students write a letter to themselves imagining it's the end of the year describing how they had changed during the year to become "that person who will have done all she wished to do or become everything he wanted to be." Zander said he wanted them to "fall passionately in love" with the person they wrote about in the letter. This kind of exercise focuses on the more joyous future we can create, and can help us conceive of the actions we need to take today to get there.

Ideal readership for this book are readers who want to conquer their fears and experience new possibilities, parents, perfectionists who are afraid of failing or being less than perfect, folks interested in self-development, and those who feel stuck in a routine and want more adventure in their lives. The author says she came from an Asian culture in which failure was unacceptable and shameful to the entire family. If she received a C on her report card, her mother told her not to come home.

If you are looking for an encouraging and engaging read written in layman's, not therapists', language by a regular person who models taking intelligent risks to melt away fears, this may be a five star read for you. "Fear isn't an end point, but the point of entry to a life of incomparable joy." Sounds promising. I enjoyed reading this book and am thinking about what fears I want to conquer by the end of the year.

title: No depth of knowledge about living with Bernese Mountain Dogs
text:
I call this book a "Cookie Cutter Book".

It's very pretty, well written and doesn't contain any depth of knowledge of this breed (other than some research into breed history).

Don't let the colorfully written breed history fool you. You could buy a generic dog training book and get as much out of it as you would from this book.

It bugs me when people seek to profit from the rising popularity of the Bernese Mountain Dog breed, especially without having made any significant investment in this breed, as this book obviously does.

This book was written by a journalist with some experience in dog training - without any profound experience in Bernese Mountain Dog breed.

There is nothing "essential" about this guide, as it relates to Bernese Mountain Dogs. It's very generic, in its application to pet owners (or aspiring breeders).

If you want an essential guide to Bernese Mountain Dogs, there are much, much more informative books available that were written by experienced breeders - people with great personal investment in the Bernese Mountain Dog breed.

My favorite for pet buyers is Julia Crawford's "BMD: An Owner's Guide to a Happy, Healthy Pet". Julia bred & exhibited Berners for more than 30 years and she's a past BMDCA Club President. Excellent book for pet buyers. Julia knows this breed well.

Next on my list is Bernd Guenther's "BMD: Dog of Destiny". If ever there were a definitive book on Berner breed type, this book offers it. He has tremendous longevity in this breed and he's an excellent photographer. This book is great for pet owners looking for more understanding of this breed and its diversity.

Another excellent book is Sharon Chestnut Smith's "The New BMD". She forged the famous "October" kennel in Berners. This book contains a lot of good information that's very relevant to our breed even today.

One last suggestion is Jude Simmond's "The Complete BMD". Jude is a longtime breeder and exhibitor in Berners and has a wealth of breed knowledge and experience. She pours a lot of her practical understanding of the BMD breed in this well written book.

If you want a dog training book, get one of those.

But if you don't mind buying a book written about a breed that the writer has little personal experience with, and you want to risk learning from someone who doesn't know this breed intimately, then perhaps this is the book for you. It is well written, after all.

title: Skillful blend of dystopian and crime fiction
text:
Michael is a highly skilled man. Skilled at burglary and various crimes. But, eventually, the law catches up with him, all while he lie sleeping. He wakes from a coma to learn that the justice system has completely changed, and his life will never be the same. Their are steps Michael must complete in order to completely re-enter society, and he has a difficult time following the rules. Will he be able to change in time to save his own life?

I found the premise of this book fascinating, and not all that difficult to imagine. I think that a scenario like this, involving a total rehaul of the penal system, is entirely plausible. In Michael, we see a character who really has to go through a rebirth of sorts. Not only has everything changed, but to him (having been in a coma) the change seems as if overnight. While everyone else has had time to adjust, Michael is in do or die mode, and it makes for an interesting internal conflict.

There is not a lot of external action in the book, a few conflicts between Michael and other characters. The story more focuses on that internal conflict, so the book has a much more pensive feel than readers might anticipate. I also think that the potentially prophetic nature of the book can make readers a bit squirmy. However, it will appeal to fans of dystopian fiction, and crime fiction, as it artfully blends the two genres.

title: Review of Davies' 'Memories'
text:
This book isn't poorly written, but it's too esoteric to appeal to a large audience. Davies himself admits this is a book 'for practioners'. The work begins by addressing the basic problems of biblical history, then looks at the problems of biblical archaeology. It closes with a detailed consideration of the maximalist-minimalist debate present in contemporary biblical studies.

'Memories' is just lucid enough to be readable, and is more interesting to someone who has read a few histories of Israel. I even recognized some of the names he mentioned (Barton, Lemche). However, this is ultimately a book that has too little to offer to a wide audience.

Though I would have loved to keep reading and hear her story about the years since she was selected to play Mary Poppins, I guess that will have to wait. I do hope that Julie Andrews will indulge all of us loyal fans once again (or more) with a continuation of her life story. I had a front row seat to see her in Victor/Victoria on Broadway in 1997 and thoroughly enjoyed seeing this legend in person. Now, as then, bravo, Julie!

title: Not So Much For Me.
text:
I hate to say that when it comes to my cooking, the recipes have to be absurdly easy! I need my recipes to have plain old basic, inexpensive ingredients that I keep in the pantry or refrigerator/freezer on a regular basis. I don't want to have to buy a bunch of ingredients that I will only use in a single recipe, and then the rest will waste. If I was more organized, I would find more recipes to use those ingredients up, but I don't. Cooking is usually not my favorite thing to do(although I do like it in spells), so I like to keep it quick and easy. I tell you all of that just so you get an idea of whether or not YOU would like this cookbook. I honestly believe that there are PLENTY of people that would greatly enjoy it!

I really want to experiment with some of the recipes throughout Farm Fresh Southern Cooking: Straight from the Garden to Your Dinner Table and see how they will do with some substitutions. I've had pretty good luck with substitutions in the past, but I've also had horrible luck, too! I had a very difficult time trying to find recipes that I would even want to make. I kept running up on ingredients like peppercorns, wine, orange liqueur, sorghum syrup, and plenty of other things that I've either never heard of or just don't keep in my house. I know some of you are probably thinking I'm pretty sad right now! ;) Again, I like to keep things simple!

There's pictures throughout, but not with every recipe. A good bit of the pictures are simply pictures of vegetables or fruit as decoration for the pages. That's not a complaint! I very much liked the pictures.

Overall, I'd say if you like to experiment a good bit with your cooking, give this one a try. I am in no way trying to give this one a bad review! If I was more experimental, I'm guessing my thoughts would be way more excited about it. It has great reviews from what I've seen.

*Thanks to Thomas Nelson Publishers for my review copy in exchange for my honest opinion.

title: Intriguing Novel, but Leaves Me Confused as to the Author's Perspective
text: TWO SISTERS is at once an autobiographical reminiscence interspersed with a fictional  tale based on the ancient world about two sisters with a passionate attraction to one another.  At one level the novel gives Vidal the chance to settle old scores against his contemporaries - Mailer, Nabokov - while allowing him the chance, in middle age, to look back on his younger self in 1948.  At another level TWO SISTERS reveals the author's fondness for testing the limits of so-called 'propriety' in the novel, particularly where sexual matters are concerned.  He has a jaundiced view of contemporary (i.e. post-1945) American culture, which he believes is both repressive and inflated in its view of itself.  However I can't help but get the feeling that the novel represents another performance on Vidal's part, where he deliberately seeks to reconstruct his public personality as a critic concerned to make an impression on his readers, using every means - stylistic, thematic, and linguistic - at his disposal.  Gore Vidal is concerned to sustain the myth of 'Gore Vidal,' leaving us to wonder whether there is anything beneath that surface, or whether he wants to remain confined within his mediatic and literary creation.

title: Well worth reading!
text:
In this second entry into this series, Persephone Alcmdei is living with her grandmother and Beverly, the young daughter of Persephone's friend who was killed in VICIOUS CIRCLE. This book involved several ongoing plots and previous characters from VICIOUS CIRCLE. They consisted of her exploration of her deepening feelings for Johnny, a werewolf and supposed King of the Wolves, her elderly witch grandmother that lives with her, her new relationship with young Beverly, her deceased friends daughter, the Eximium and her nomination as High Priestess, the fairies, Menessos and of course her acceptance of her destiny as the Lustrata.

Johnny, is living in Persephone`s home. He has convinced Persephone that she is the Lustrata and as the Lustrata his pack is hers to summon as she needs. She is an advocate for the waerwolves and writes a column about them and provides kenneling in her basement for when they turn furry and need a safe place to stay. Persephone is also trying to come to terms with the vampire mark "the stain" as she calls it, that she received from Menessos in VICIOUS CIRCLE and her unwilling attraction to Menessos.

Persephone receives a phone call from Lydia, a coven witch, who has nominated Persephone for the position of High Priestess. At her grandmothers urging, she agrees to apply for the position. After all, Persephone is the Lustrata and she will need a close relationship with the Coven Elders. The witch chosen for the High Priestess involves the Eximium, which is a series of tests set forth by the Elders. During the course of the Eximium, witches are murdered and the police are called in. The resolution of the murders is quickly resolved in approximately one third of the book. The first of the book is her relationships with her family and Johnny, the second part is the Eximium and the third is the final confrontation with the fairies.

What is it I like about this book? There frankly, is not a lot of action. She isn't a kick butt heroine that is featured so prominently in urban fantasy, but I enjoyed it. I think it has to be the characters and the storytelling, which are both very interesting. I like Persephone; she seems real, even as a witch. She isn't all kick butt, take no prisoners, she is approachable, and likeable. Her character grows and makes for a very interesting and fast read. I will definitely read the next books in this

title: BLACK dots too dark for Bullet Journal layouts...the same contrast as shown on the cover near the spine.
text:
It comes with 2 index pages (double-sided) in the front, BUT...the dots are black. As in BLACK. If you made a grid with 2 dots per cm using a black Sharpie fine-tip pen, that's what this looks like. The individual dot has a circumference of 1mm.
The description says "light black dots"...so I was expecting that they would be faint and inobtrusive, as other dot journals are. I suppose I can look at the description now and say that if they were going to be inobtrusive, they would have said "gray" dots, but so many products are made-in-China/described by non-native-speakers (in English), that I've learned that such nuances are often missing, and you have to take the description as best you can.

So the interior is a black polka-dot grid, which is much too dark for most conventional bullet journals, where the dots provide 'almost invisible' guidance for text, diagrams, graphs, lettering, etc. If I hold the book at arm's length, the dots are very obvious (the usual dots in dot journals are actually very faint, allowing users to use them as guides, and then disappear visually beneath the actual journaling. These dots are very visible no matter what.
There is a 1/2 inch white border around the outer edges of the page.

Even if I used a black pen, the dots would make it too busy to be clear and too obstructive to use in traditional bullet journal layouts. If, however, you just want to make a grid out of he entire page, then this might work for you. But then you'd probably be buying graph paper.

Also, as a glue-bound book, it will be impossible to get the book to lie flat. I was planning to remove the binding and hole-punch the individual pages and use them in a mini-binder.

I returned it.

title: Has the makings of a cult book
text:
This book is going to have a small, but fanatical, audience. To find out if you will like this book take the following survey.
1. How important is cycling in your life? (0-50 points)
2. How interested are you in things English? (0-25 points)
3. How eccentric are you? (0-25 points)

We don't learn much about the author. His parents were communists, he went to Oxford, he's a poet, he loves bicycles, and he's a bit of a ladies man. He also seems to be a bit older than me.

What we do learn is the history of English amateur and professional cycling. There are stories about bicycle clubs that are 100 years old, about record setting attempts, amateur racing, professional racing, and just good old touring and club rides. There are stories from the big tours and classics that are better told than in any of the official histories. I don't know exactly how old Tim Hilton is, but he recounts watching Fausto Coppi at an exhibition race in London in 1958.

The book seems to ramble a bit - like an epic bike ride. Tim has been riding a long and glorious time and has a lot to say. All of it is worth listening to. One day I'd like to meet Tim. Heck, one day I'd like to be Tim. But then I'm English, I love cycling, and people say I'm quite odd.

text:
Warning: This review reveals the ending of the book.

Lets just start by saying this novel is entirely too long. I have no problem with long books, but there needs to be a reason. We learn a lot about each character, which is fun, but in the end I am not sure it really helped move the story along given that the ending of the story was so weak. King definitely needed the help of an editor.

My biggest complaint is the end of the story. The only thing I can equate it to is the age old TV disappointment - the entire show was really just a dream. King's ending leaves the story without a point. There is no reason for all of the pain the characters have been put through. Baby aliens just like to play with those creatures that are smaller than them, like our kids and bugs. Really? I spent all that time reading for that? And, if that was the point, the futility and senselessness of life, there needed to be more of a punch to drive it home.

title: Jack Reacher:  An anti-hero for today's times and crimes
text:
I am a big fan of Barry Eisler's John Rain series. Rain, the half-American, half Japanese, jazz-and-whisky loving assassin for hire is one of the great anti-heroes of modern fiction, and Eisler writes a fight scene and an exotic locale as well as anyone. A friend who has also read the Rain novels recommended that I read Lee Child's Jack Reacher series: "John Rain is cool jazz, and that's fine, but Reacher is Stevie Ray Vaughan, and he rocks."

While that may have not been the most poetic reference ever, it worked. Lee Child's "Killing Floor," the first Jack Reacher novel, had me hooked from page one.

With a minimum of exposition, Child drops Reacher and the reader pell-mell into a murder investigation on the first page, with Reacher as the defendant. Reacher, a former Army brat and military policeman now wandering the South as a dischargee, may not be the murderer, but he sure as heck ain't innocent. As he says, they can't prove I did it, because I hadn't killed anyone . . . in a while.

The murder investigation quickly morphs into a life-or-death struggle to break an international criminal conspiracy hidden behind the bucolic streets and manicured lawns of Margrave, Georgia. Unfortunately for the criminals, Reacher learns that he has a personal involvement in breaking this conspiracy, and Reacher is not an investigator to play nice or by the rules. Child may rely a bit too much on coincidence to get Reacher involved (Reacher just happens to randomly pick a town to wander through in time to find himself named as the initial suspect in the murder of his brother, a talented Treasury investigator who was also trying to bust the criminal ring). But since the coincidences are more in the set-up of the novel than the resolution, they are more or less forgiveable.

Reacher brings a keen mind and a brutal streak a mile wide to his investigation. Partnering with an aging yet still hale detective and a beautiful cop, Reacher soon finds himself immersed in a conspiracy where the perpetrators use ghastly torture and murder to further their own agenda . . . including offing their own members to keep the others in line.

The only problem for the criminals is that Reacher may be the only person in Georgia who can take the criminals' level of violence and go one level deeper. As a career MP, Reacher was trained to go after AWOL Rangers, Seals, and special forces guys and bring them back. As a result, you're not going to find a more capable guy with a gun, knife, sap, or his bare hands (or other lethal body parts). And Child gives Reacher several chances to use his training to the utmost. These fight scenes are written very well, as are Reacher's investigation and his preparation for the fights.

A complex plot offers a lot of insight into the corrupt world of international currency and counterfeiting, and while Child's characters may not offer the nuances of Tolstoy, they are a well-rounded, well-written group that generally avoids cliche. Mercifully, Child's characters are smart enough to figure out what's going on independently, and we are generally spared those scenes where the villains tell the heroes about their criminal activities in order to fill in the gaps. And while the setting of Margrave, Georgia, may not be as exotic as Eisler's use of Tokyo or other haunts in Southeast Asia, Child writes the South very well and gives it a haunting menace appropriate to the story.

A brutal story, "Killing Floor" is nevertheless first and foremost an intelligent thriller that does not get overwhelmed by its considerable blood and violence. The story unfolds gradually, and loops back on itself a couple of times as solid conjectures have to get reexamined in light of new facts.

While "Killing Floor" will never be accused of being Great Literature, it is a heck of a read and it is easy to see why so many devoted fans have checked out the on-going series. Count me in as another reader eager to see where Reacher's wanderings will take him.

title: Great and Important Book for Kids!
text:
Great Holiday Gift!
Summary:
This is a very, very touching book. Maria did a great, great job in writing a touching story that comes to life from our own experiences. It is a collectors book, beautifully illustrated, and a quick, easy read. So, it is in truth a wonderful children's book that many adults would love to read. It is a "Kleenix" book - make sure you have a box available when you read it.
The Story:
The story features a little girl, Kate, who meets a little boy, Timmy, who has challenges doing the things that we all take for granted. Kate asks her Mom, "Why is that boy different?" Kate is afraid to initiate speaking with him, and is at a loss for what to do. Her Mommy explains to Kate, that when Timmy was born, his Mommy cried a lot of tears because Timmy was hurt when he was born. The story blossoms from there.
After working up all of her courage, and fumbling quite a bit, Kate meets the boy and finds out that he is a really great kid, and has hope, and dreams, and thoughts and feelings and fears like all other children. Kate realizes that Timmy, is just like her. From there on Kate goes out of her way to make sure that Timmy is included in her activities with her friends.
The Story's Importance:
This is very important for all children (and adults) to learn more about others who are different than us as well as to learn more of their perspective. We have a handicapped child, yet, I am still uncomfortable about how to first greet a handicapped, or challenged person when we first meet them, because I never want to intrude, or impose.. With that in mind, I can see how it very challenging for someone who has had no exposure to people who are handicapped, challenged, or just different. I wish I read this book when I was a child, because I am no different than anyone else in learning about how to meet someone with disabilities.
Real Life example:
Our daughter (...) is severely handicapped with cerebral palsy, is six years old, and attends a full-inclusion kindergarten classroom. (...) (She) has been very fortunate to have made some great friends at school and out of school. But, most children (and adults) do not know what to do, or say when they first meet her.
We always introduce (her) to her new friends, and explain that when she was born, she got hurt. And, while (she) is very bright, like they are, but her body can't do the things she wants to do. It's kind of like when their foot falls asleep and it becomes difficult to walk! (Her) friends relate to this and are no longer afraid of her, or of doing something wrong. Her friends often argue over who will play with (her) or help her. Now (she) has many very good friends who play with her at school and come to the house, as well.
Christmas Gifts:
The book is a great holiday gift. We thought it is so touching, and informative, we purchased about a dozen to give to (our daughter)'s therapists (touching), and her teachers (informative). We also kept a few for our family for our own teary enjoyment!

title: Presidential History Buffs, check this out !
text:
I highly enjoyed this book , being a cross between the history of the White House ,and a slice of life from 21 different Presidents who lived there . It tells of the White House , from when John Adams moved in, while the walls weren't all finished yet , through different decoration-changes during the years. There were some Presidents who didn't change much of anything as far as the building goes, but others ( many times due to their wives , ) wanted to redo certain rooms, the furniture, painting , china, etc . It tells of the additions of improvements, such as an indoor "water closet" , on up to more modern improvements such as electricity ,telephones, radios ,television, etc . , and of the changes in what the specific rooms were used for during different time frames.
This was also interesting ,as the author chose 21 presidents to tell of, one per chapter. He told of some of their work-related life, but also of their family relationships , and what type of personality they had , how they handled tragedies and triumphs , and which ones loved entertaining guests, and others who preferred to have privacy as often as possible .
I listened to this on audio ,and will have to say that I only listened to a few chapters at a time, then read something else for a break . I think to listen to it all in one go, would make your mind go a bit numb ,and you would just use it as background noise . So, in order for me to get the most out of it and pay attention to it , I needed a short break throughout . The author also narrated it and did a really nice job on it .
All in all, though, if you like history, especially about our presidents and White House, I think you'd find this right up your alley .

text:
This Sneaky Chef cookbook can be purchased at a ridiculously low price! Even if you only find one recipe to love it is worth buying. I tried the "Stuffed Manli-Cotti" which is manicotti with hidden vegetables. Yes it takes a bit more effort to steam the veggies but if you do it the day before you can easily sneak them into the food without anyone noticing.

Unfortunately my husband got home right when I was going to put tofu in the cheese mixture so I decided to just use double the ricotta which turned out great. I think he would have suspected something if I'd used the tofu. Already you are putting peeled zucchini and cauliflower in the tomato sauce and in the cheese - 1 cup in each.

This dish is not the easiest dish to make - you have to fill up manicotti tubes which tends to be tricky. You can however save time on the recipe if you just use a large jar of Prego with tomato and basil instead of the homemade sauce. That way you don't have to make a third recipe. I consider making the "white puree" a day before a recipe too.

The only things I really changed in the recipe was the amount of salt. It needed a full teaspoon not half a teaspoon. I also used ½ cup of parmesan cheese instead of 6 tablespoons. Then I doubled the ricotta as mentioned before.

Anyway, I loved the recipe and will make it again. I'm looking forward to trying other recipes. These look interesting:

Mint Chocolate Chip Ice Cream - This uses up bananas - freeze them before they go bad
Berry Crisp - Uses frozen mixed berries
Doctor's Choice Chili - Uses two types of puree
Pesto Mashed Potatoes
Major Leek Soup

While I survived making the recipes with a mini-food processor you really might want the real thing. [[ASIN:B00004S9EM Cuisinart DLC-10S Pro Classic 7-Cup Food Processor]]

~The Rebecca Review

title: This was a fun, quick
text:
This book is the first in the series Wicked Witches of the Midwest, by Amanda M. Lee, Published December 12th 2012 by Winchester Shaw Publications. Narrated by Aris.

The genre of this book is paranormal, modern detective, fantasy and magic. Which are all my favorites.

This is a story of the Winchester family, a family of witches that consists of an old aunt (don’t let that fool you, she is quit handful), three middle aged sisters, each one has a daughter (three cousins). Bay Winchester is working as the local editor of Hemlock Cove’s only newspaper, while her two cousins Clove and Thistle work in a shop. A murder happens in the town, and Bay feels she can be in benefit in more than one way, with the help of her family, the town’s sheriff, and a biker, she will solve this case.

This was a fun, quick, and enjoyable story, once I started it was hard to leave it (I ended up listening to it in one day). I do, however, have to admit the setting had some big holes in it that left me wondering. The whole town knows that there is a family of witches, and all they do is gaze uncomfortably at them?? Or what kind of sheriff asks the local witch to accompany him to the crime scene?? Yet I felt that the characters were real and believable enough, they were likable. I mean it’s a family of seven women, their bickering and fighting made sense to me (as I’m living in four women family so I know). Although they weren’t as deep as I would have liked. The events were told by the narrative rather than shown, and while the story was fast paced and fun, the characters were kind of predictable and (there wasn’t a lot of events there to start with), interesting, but somehow kind of dull.

The narrator Aris did an excellent job with the story, I mostly enjoyed the bickering of the girls, she made it very fun and realistic at the same time, each character had its own accent and tone. Her voice gave the action parts more realism and made them far more interesting than reading. Needless to say I will be looking forward to listen to the second book, and I think I will be finishing this series.

title: Interesting, if quirky and jerky, thriller
text:
Dr. Frank Clevenger is a forensic psychiatrist who could use a psychiatrist of his own. Oh wait, he has one. But he only has time for one visit while tracking down a serial killer who expertly dissects a single aspect of his victim's body.

The backstories in "The Architect" are distracting and really don't add anything. Clevenger is an alcoholic. That addicition inteferes with his bonding with Billy Bishop, a 19 year old recently adopted by Clevenger. Adopt a teenager? Young Bishop's problems with his own early fatherhood, drug and alcohol consumption keep disracting Clevenger - and the reader - from the pursuit of the murderer, And then there's the ongoing off-and-on affair with Whitney McCormick, Clevenger's FBI boss and occasional lover. Again a distraction. Finally author Ablow inserts his political opinions into the narrative. Yet another disctraction.

Ignore these things and Ablow crafts a reasonably interesting story. West Crosse is a brilliant architect. Educated at Yale, he is a member of the Skull and Bones, the secret society so beloved of conspiracists. His Skull and Bones membership and referrals bring him new commissions. Crosse designs to reflect the innermost desires of his clients, even those desires the clients repress. Crosse wants perfection for his clients, not only in the structures he designs for them, but in their lives. So as author quickly makes apparent, Crosse more or less redesigns his client's families as well by getting rid of those elements he finds disturbing.

Crosse is definitely a bit off the beaten track in a less accomplished way then Hannibal Lechter was. Clevenger applies his forensic psychiatric skills in identifying Crosse as a suspect. This, frankly, happens a bit too easily and is less than credible. But it works because Ablow's storytelling skills are pretty good.

Overall, if you ignore the backstories and the author's political pontifications, Ablow has created a gruesome killer, a moderately interesting chase and an overblown, but enjoyable, climax. Not a bad read at all.

Jerry

title: Love, jealousy, and a slip of the tongue.
text:
Girl in the Blue Coat is an excellent piece of historical fiction that tells the poignant story of a young girl coping with loss and struggling to survive during the Nazi occupation. The author does a masterful job of detailing personal tragedy in the midst of the larger, worldwide tragedy that was World War II. Her narrow focus on this one young girl and her struggles serves to amplify the tragedy of war by exposing its far reaching and unexpected victims that were often far from the battlefield.

This story moves along at a fast pace, building suspense and taking the reader through some truly unexpected twists and turns. This has all the fine plotting of a mystery, and all the period detail to transport the reader back to a time when food was scarce, people were disappearing, loved ones were dying, and there were only hints of atrocities in other countries. This is a truly gripping tale that explored the nature of grief, guilt, and war. A small story told on a large stage, The Girl in the Blue Coat is a must read.
